## Where This Fits
This week puts the attention of W3 back into a **trainable model**, and faces for the first time what actually happens when you train one. The organising frame is the **residual stream**: each token owns a shared communication bus, and every layer reads part of it, computes, and adds its result back — the $\mathbf{X}$ of W3 is called the residual stream from here on. The frame returns in W6 (replacing some layers with SSMs), W8 (LoRA as a low-rank bypass) and W14 (circuits and SAEs); it is the single most reusable idea in the course. Two things happen on the board: **parameter accounting** (turning last week's $24d^2$ into $N \approx 12\,n_{\text{layer}} d^2 + Vd$, then inverting it on a real model's `config.json` and explaining the error) and the **pre-LN vs. post-LN Jacobian** (the sequel to the three Jacobians of W1). The compute ledger receives its **optimizer-state** row this week, counted all the way to bytes — that number is the motivation for W8. **The block is assembled live by the instructor** (demo 1, on top of W3's attention); the training runs and the instability reproduction are rehearsed in advance and replayed in class. You do not need to run anything.

## Learning Objectives
1. Write out the forward pass of a pre-LN Transformer block (residual stream, two sub-layers, RMSNorm, gated FFN) and **account for its parameters term by term**; derive $N \approx 12\,n_{\text{layer}} d^2 + Vd$ from the accounting, invert it in class on a real open-weight model's `config.json`, and **name the sources of the error** (GQA, $n_{\text{head}} d_{\text{head}} \neq d$, the $d_{\text{ff}}/d$ ratio, tied or untied embeddings).
2. Write the layer-to-layer Jacobian for pre-LN and for post-LN, explain why the former contains an identity term and the latter does not; state the price of pre-LN (the residual norm accumulates with depth, so deep layers make relatively smaller updates) and what the 2024–2025 return of post-norm (Gemma 2, OLMo 2, Peri-LN) is repairing.
3. Explain "every layer is an additive update" from the residual-stream view, use it to predict the shape of the curve in demo 3 (which layers are cheap to remove and which are not), and state the three qualifications on that "robustness" (middle layers only, on some metrics only, usually with healing).
4. Write SwiGLU in its three-matrix form, explain that $\frac{8}{3}d$ is an **iso-parameter convention** rather than a law, and state that gated FFNs beating ReLU FFNs is an empirical result with weak theory behind it.
5. Write the AdamW update, explain how decoupled weight decay differs from L2 regularisation, and count the optimizer state in bytes (about 16 bytes per parameter in mixed precision) — hence why full fine-tuning of an 8B model does not fit in 64 GB, the entry point to W8.
6. Diagnose the three symptoms of training instability (loss spikes, attention-logit growth, output-logit divergence), state the diagnostic order (**statistics first, data second**), and pair each symptom with a mitigation (QK-norm / soft-capping / QK-clip, z-loss, clipping and warmup).
7. State what muP claims (zero-shot hyperparameter transfer across width), its known limits (depth, MoE and industrial scale), and the update rule and current status of Muon-style matrix optimizers (the new default of 2025–2026, still under validation).

## Demos
Three programs again, all built on last week's. **You are not required to run anything** — the numbers on the slides are the rehearsal records checked in with the code — but the code is published so that you can read it, re-run it, and change it. Each folder's `README.md` gives requirements, setup, commands, and what you should see; the index at [`demos/`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos) explains the shared environment.

| | Slide | What it shows | Needs | Runs on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Demo 1 · RMSNorm → SwiGLU → Block → GPT; invert `config.json`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w04_d1_block_scratch) | p16, p20, p22 | A Transformer block assembled from zero on top of W3's attention, checked by three tests; `count_params.py` turns a real `config.json` into three columns — the $12\,n_{\text{layer}}d^2 + Vd$ approximation, a term-by-term exact count, and what the safetensors files actually store — for Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen3-0.6B (exact = stored, to the parameter); a replayed training run of the 4.8 M-parameter tiny GPT on the W1 Shakespeare text, with its bits-per-byte next to W1's n-grams | `torch` only; the two models in the local cache for `count`; the Shakespeare text for training | tests and `count` on any laptop; training on Apple silicon (`mps`), ≈ 9 min — replay needs nothing |
| [Demo 2 · training instability on the tiny GPT](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w04_d2_instability) | p29, p44 | Replay only. Three recorded settings: 16-layer pre-LN vs. post-LN with no warmup; a learning-rate sweep $\{1, 3, 10\}\times$ tracking loss, $\max\lvert s_{ij}\rvert$, $\log Z$ and gradient norms; the highest rate again with QK-norm. What appeared was entropy collapse rather than a spike, and QK-norm turned the stuck run into a learning one | `torch` only; demo 1's code | `replay` on any laptop; re-running the 38 minutes of training as demo 1 |
| [Demo 3 · skip one layer at a time, measure the perplexity](https://github.com/hungshinlee/NLP-LLM/tree/main/demos/w04_d3_layer_removal) | p32 | Qwen3-0.6B on a Chinese paragraph and its English translation; each of the 28 layers in turn is made an identity by a forward hook and the perplexity re-measured — the first three layers are catastrophic, the middle is cheap, the last layer costs only ×2.5, and layers 16–18 matter only for the Chinese text | `torch` + `transformers`, Qwen3-0.6B (from W3 demo 3) | any laptop with ~3 GB free RAM (`mps` or `--device cpu`) |

Tested on one machine only — an Apple M5 Max (64 GB, no CUDA), macOS 27.0, Python 3.12 — with the versions pinned in `demos/versions.lock`. "Any laptop" means the code depends on nothing platform-specific, not that it was verified elsewhere. Terminal prompts are in Chinese; Enter advances, `q` quits.

## References
- **JM3** ch 7 *Transformers and Pretraining* (second half: the full block, the residual stream, training)
- **RAS** ch 4 (the full GPT block — the skeleton of demo 1) and the first half of ch 5 (the training loop); **BB**, the optimization and regularization chapters; **UDL** ch 12 (Transformers)
- Elhage et al., **A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits**, Transformer Circuits Thread, December 2021 — **a research report from Anthropic, not a peer-reviewed paper**; the source of "the residual stream is a communication channel" and of virtual weights
- Veit, Wilber & Belongie, **Residual Networks Behave Like Ensembles of Relatively Shallow Networks**, NIPS 2016 (arXiv:1605.06431) — why additive updates tolerate the removal of a layer: the original argument, on ResNets
- Xiong et al., **On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture**, ICML 2020 (arXiv:2002.04745) — the gradient analysis of pre-LN vs. post-LN; "pre-LN needs no warmup" is this paper's claim
- Zhang & Sennrich, **Root Mean Square Layer Normalization**, NeurIPS 2019 (arXiv:1910.07467) — re-centering is not what makes LayerNorm work
- Kim et al., **Peri-LN: Revisiting Normalization Layer in the Transformer Architecture**, ICML 2025 (arXiv:2502.02732) — the variance growth of pre-LN, and normalizing the sub-layer output as well
- Gemma Team, **Gemma 2: Improving Open Language Models at a Practical Size**, arXiv:2408.00118 (2024) — both pre- and post-norm, and logit soft-capping (both in the body; the abstract mentions only local-global attention and GQA)
- OLMo Team, **2 OLMo 2 Furious**, arXiv:2501.00656 (2024; a shorter version at COLM 2025) — a public recipe that combines reordered norm, QK-norm and z-loss (details in the body, not in the abstract)
- Zhu et al., **Transformers without Normalization**, CVPR 2025 (arXiv:2503.10622) — DyT: the counter-evidence, replacing Norm with $\tanh(\alpha x)$
- Shazeer, **GLU Variants Improve Transformer**, arXiv:2002.05202 (2020) — SwiGLU, and the iso-parameter comparison behind $\frac{8}{3}$
- Geva et al., **Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories**, EMNLP 2021 (arXiv:2012.14913) — the memory view of the FFN; the prequel to W14
- Gromov et al., **The Unreasonable Ineffectiveness of the Deeper Layers**, arXiv:2403.17887 (2024; v2 is the ICLR camera-ready) — removing deep layers costs little on QA-style benchmarks, with healing; the reference point for demo 3
- Men et al., **ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect**, arXiv:2403.03853 (2024) — layer removal by a block-influence score
- Kingma & Ba, **Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization**, ICLR 2015 (arXiv:1412.6980)
- Loshchilov & Hutter, **Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization**, ICLR 2019 (arXiv:1711.05101) — AdamW; L2 and weight decay are not equivalent under Adam
- Rajbhandari et al., **ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models**, arXiv:1910.02054 (2019) — the source of the 16-bytes-per-parameter accounting under mixed precision
- Wortsman et al., **Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities**, arXiv:2309.14322 (2023) — **the one paper on training stability that can really be taught**; the design basis of demo 2
- Zhai et al., **Stabilizing Transformer Training by Preventing Attention Entropy Collapse**, ICML 2023 (arXiv:2303.06296) — announced in W3, picked up here
- Henry et al., **Query-Key Normalization for Transformers**, Findings of EMNLP 2020 (arXiv:2010.04245) — the original source of QK-norm
- Dehghani et al., **Scaling Vision Transformers to 22 Billion Parameters**, arXiv:2302.05442 (2023) — the most-cited use of QK-norm in large-scale training
- Chowdhery et al., **PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways**, arXiv:2204.02311 (2022) — the source of z-loss; the loss-spike and "skip the batch" experience is in the body
- Takase et al., **Spike No More: Stabilizing the Pre-training of Large Language Models**, COLM 2025 (arXiv:2312.16903) — another spike mechanism: sub-layer outputs that are large relative to the shortcut
- Yang et al., **Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer**, NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv:2203.03466) — muP
- Bordelon et al., **Depthwise Hyperparameter Transfer in Residual Networks: Dynamics and Scaling Limit**, arXiv:2309.16620 (2023); Dey et al., **Don't be lazy: CompleteP enables compute-efficient deep transformers**, arXiv:2505.01618 (2025) — transfer across depth; the two papers scale the residual branch by different powers
- Blake et al., **u-μP: The Unit-Scaled Maximal Update Parametrization**, arXiv:2407.17465 (2024) — muP combined with unit scaling and low precision
- Zhou et al., **How to Set the Learning Rate for Large-Scale Pre-training?**, arXiv:2601.05049 (2026) — questions whether μTransfer scales to industrial sizes and to MoE
- Jordan et al., **Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks**, 2024-12-08 — **a blog post by Keller Jordan, not a paper**; the definition of Muon and the rule that embeddings and output layers stay on AdamW
- Liu et al., **Muon is Scalable for LLM Training**, arXiv:2502.16982 (2025) — Moonshot's scaling of Muon to LLM size
- Bai et al., **Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence**, arXiv:2507.20534 (2025, technical report) — MuonClip and QK-clip; the abstract claims zero loss spikes over 15.5T tokens
- DeepSeek, **DeepSeek V4 Technical Documentation** (model card, 2026-04-27) — **a specification document, not a paper**; states that Muon is used, and that the residual connection is modified by mHC
- Hyper-connections (several learnable, mixed residual streams): search *Hyper-Connections residual stream*, *manifold-constrained hyper-connections*
- Qwen3 dropping the QKV bias and adding QK-norm: search *Qwen3 technical report QK-Norm*
- The Adam-side reason for warmup: search *RAdam variance of the adaptive learning rate warmup*
- Kaplan's $N$ excludes embeddings: Kaplan et al. 2020 in the W7 references, §2.1
